job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Hassan Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Hassan. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me the public view and the private one. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Packed. I'm doing a master's in software engineering at Gresham, and I live at home with my parents and two younger sisters. I'm up before dawn for prayer, then I code with an AI assistant open all morning, and I'm in class after lunch. Evenings I sell small tools I build, like a stock sheet for tile importers, and I help my father with his tile import business.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your degree, and how did it go?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer science, a pass. I spent more time on my side business than on exams, which cost me marks. I had no internship because I was too busy with my own thing, and I know how that sounds to an employer, but my sales records are real and they're my best proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what a sensible person expected. Every new thing gets sold as a revolution and then settles into a tool. I'd tell my friends to keep building and selling, because value is value whatever the buzz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. I use AI every day and I'd keep using it, and my small tools keep earning about 700 a month. The pressure is that I've a pass degree and a loan of about 11,000, and employers like grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and keep selling tools to tile importers and other small traders. I'd apply to software firms that value shipped products. And I'd save half of what I earn, because my father always says a man should keep a reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Steady, with a little itch to do more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the tile tool earn money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small monthly fee, 15 a month per shop. I have 40 customers now, mostly through my father's contacts. They used to track stock on paper and lose track of containers. A tool that saves a shop owner one lost container pays for itself for a whole year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the pass degree really a problem for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less than for others, because I've something to show. But it will close some doors, like the big graduate schemes. I'd rather open my own door than knock on theirs and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for people who are ready, and a risk for people who wait. I'd tell my friends to learn the tools now and start something small. Markets reward those who move, and I'd say that online, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit uneasy. Tools will make small software cheaper, which hits my own sales. And big firms will hire fewer juniors. But I'm better placed than most because I already sell something and use these tools daily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen from tile importers to other small traders, like furniture and spare parts, and use AI to build the tools faster. I'd keep my prices low and my customers many. I'd also keep applying for jobs, as a backup, in case the tools market gets crowded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert. Like standing on the platform when the train is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said tools will make small software cheaper. How does that hit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a shop owner can ask an assistant to make their own stock sheet, my 15 a month tool is in trouble. So I need to sell service, not just software. The thing a customer pays for isn't the code, it's that I answer the phone when their system breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you have a view on who should help people who can't move as fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family and community first, then the state as a last backstop. I don't like handouts as a first answer, but I accept some support for those who can't work. My father came here with nothing and built a business, so I believe in effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a shock and that our families, our neighbourhoods and our mosques have to look after each other first. I'd also say that the governments should not freeze businesses with panic rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened for the first time. My software business could be copied by anyone's assistant, and my pass degree wouldn't get me a job in a market that stops hiring. Only the hands-on side, like my father's tile business, would last a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my effort into the tile business, helping my father import and deliver, and I'd use AI to run the paperwork. I'd cut every unnecessary cost, and I'd keep my savings in cash and gold for a while. I'd also help my sisters think about what to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A knot in the gut. I'd stay up, then I'd start making lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your father's business would last longer. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tiles are heavy and real. They get unloaded, cut and laid by people, and robots for that come about 2031 on the card. I'd have three more years to learn what comes next. I'd rather own a warehouse full of tiles than a piece of software anyone can copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your sisters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older one, Leyla, wants to study law and the younger is thinking about nursing. I'd tell them to pick things that need trust and presence, and I'd be paying for part of it. That matters more to me than my own career.

Governments shouldn't freeze business with **panic rules** made in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is exactly the kind of runway a smart person uses. I'd tell my friends to build a business, own something real, and build a reserve before the date. People who panic early waste the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm quite upbeat. I'd have two or three years of selling and working before it lands. I'd be 29 with a company, maybe a few employees, savings, and ownership of some assets. I'd stay a step ahead of the tools since I use them daily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my software income into things that last, like a share in the tile warehouse and a small property. I'd hire one student to help me sell. And I'd take a job in a software firm for a year, mainly to learn how a big company works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Focused. A little competitive, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a job, if the business is going well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn things I can't learn alone, like how a big team ships and how a firm handles customers at scale. And a salary smooths the months when sales dip. A year inside a big company is worth more to me than any course I could pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'own something real' mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A share in my father's warehouse, a flat, equipment. Things that exist even if software becomes free. I'm not saying no to shares or funds, but I like to be able to walk around what I own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to build something, and I'd tell everyone to start now. A decade is long enough to learn a trade, save a deposit and raise a child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel well placed. By 34 I could run a proper firm, own property and have a family. I'm a person who uses the tools and also knows how real businesses work, and that's a good mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the business, marry within a few years, and buy a house near my parents. I'd put aside a fixed amount every month and invest in the family warehouse. I'd keep studying the tools each year, and I'd teach my sisters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confident, and grateful. A long, open road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year version that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get complacent, or take too much risk because it looks far away. My father says a long road still has holes in it. My father taught me to keep six months of expenses in the bank, however good business looks, and I'd never break that rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think will be left behind in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who can't or won't change, and people without family around them. I'd hate to see that. Our mosque already runs a small fund and I'd give more to it as I earn more.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my software business could be copied overnight and there's no time to build assets. What would help is stable rules for small businesses, cheap credit for those who want to start something, and community funds for people who can't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Perhaps that adapting fast is partly luck. I could build my own business at 19 because my father had contacts and a roof over us, and a young man without those can't just do the same.

headlineQuote: I could build my own business at 19 because my father had contacts and a roof over us, and a young man without those can't just do the same.
portrait: Hassan is 24, doing a **software engineering** master's after a pass in computer science.
He lives with his parents and two sisters in **Gresham** and sells small tools to tile importers.
Traditional and adaptive, he uses AI **every day** and trusts hard assets, family and faith.
His side income of about 700 a month and **his father's tile trade** give him a base.
His mood is mostly calm and turns **anxious** only when the timeline is two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because software can be copied and no time remains to build assets.
whatWouldHelp: **Stable rules** for small businesses, cheap credit for starters and community funds.
